data.description: The driver took a significantly longer route from Orchard Central to Changi Airport T3. I normally take the PIE which takes about 35 minutes and costs around $28. On this trip the driver went through Geylang and East Coast area, taking 37 minutes and the fare was $35. The driver did not inform me about any route change or traffic. The extra distance was 4.3 km and I was overcharged. I am requesting a refund of the excess fare.

json.requested_outcome: partial refund of the excess distance fare
json.brief: The recommended PIE route is 20.5 km and the car travelled 24.8 km, a deviation of 4.3 km, far above the 1 km tolerance [E-TRP-01] [E-RTE-01] [Section 1.3]. The GPS trace shows the car off the recommended route from the second ping at 13:17 and through Geylang and the East Coast area to Changi [E-GPS-02] [E-GPS-08] [E-GPS-11]. Section 1.2 requires the driver to tell the rider in the app chat, or aloud with a call recording, before or at the point of deviation. The only exchange about the route is the rider asking at 13:24 whether this was the right way [E-CHT-05], and the driver answering 'Don't worry, I know the way' without naming a reroute or a reason [E-CHT-06]. That is not the notice Section 1.2 asks for. The fare rose by S$6.50 and S$3.44 of it is the excess distance fare [E-PAY-01]. Section 1.3 refunds the excess distance fare when the rider was not informed of a deviation over 1 km, and Precedent 7.1 did exactly that [Precedent 7.1].

arguments.point: The deviation is 4.3 km against a recommended route of 20.5 km, over the 1 km tolerance.
No message or call told the rider about a reroute before or at the deviation; the driver's only reply came after the rider asked and gave no reason.
The remedy Section 1.3 gives for an unannounced deviation is the excess distance fare, S$3.44, as in Precedent 7.1.

weaknesses.point: The traffic record shows a vehicle fire on the PIE during the trip, so the driver will say the reroute was justified; that limits the remedy to the partial refund.

json.brief: Section 1.1 lets a driver leave the recommended path for real-time traffic. Historical traffic data, which Section 1.4 names as the test, shows a vehicle fire on the PIE eastbound from 13:05 to 13:50 with two lanes blocked [E-TRF-01] and heavy congestion at the PIE airport exit from 13:15 to 13:40 [E-TRF-02]; the trip ran 13:15 to 13:52 [E-TRP-01]. The ECP was flowing freely [E-TRF-03]. So this is the 'rerouted for traffic' row of Section 1.3, and the rider arrived in 37 minutes against an estimate of 35 [E-TRP-01]. When the rider asked, the driver answered within a minute [E-CHT-05] [E-CHT-06]. The only remedy that row gives is a partial refund of the excess distance fare, S$3.44, not the whole S$6.50 difference, and the tolls of S$2.22 pass through at cost [E-PAY-01] [Precedent 7.1].

arguments.point: A vehicle fire and heavy congestion on the PIE overlapped the trip, so the reroute had a traffic justification.
The ECP was flowing smoothly, a reasonable alternative to the blocked PIE.
A justified but unannounced reroute earns the excess distance fare only: S$3.44 of the S$6.50 difference; the S$2.22 of tolls passes through at cost.

rebuttals.reply: The deviation is not disputed, but Section 1.3 gives no refund for distance alone when the reroute is justified by traffic.
The driver reassured the rider within a minute of the question; the reply did not name the reroute, but the rider was never refused an answer.
Agreed that Precedent 7.1 applies; it also shows the refund stops at the excess distance fare.

concessions.point: No chat message or call before or at the deviation told the rider of the reroute and the reason.
The deviation of 4.3 km is over the 1 km tolerance.

rider_advocate.brief: The recommended PIE route is 20.5 km and the car travelled 24.8 km, a deviation of 4.3 km, far above the 1 km tolerance [E-TRP-01] [E-RTE-01] [Section 1.3]. The GPS trace shows the car off the recommended route from the second ping at 13:17 and through Geylang and the East Coast area to Changi [E-GPS-02] [E-GPS-08] [E-GPS-11]. Section 1.2 requires the driver to tell the rider in the app chat, or aloud with a call recording, before or at the point of deviation. The only exchange about the route is the rider asking at 13:24 whether this was the right way [E-CHT-05], and the driver answering 'Don't worry, I know the way' without naming a reroute or a reason [E-CHT-06]. That is not the notice Section 1.2 asks for. The fare rose by S$6.50 and S$3.44 of it is the excess distance fare [E-PAY-01]. Section 1.3 refunds the excess distance fare when the rider was not informed of a deviation over 1 km, and Precedent 7.1 did exactly that [Precedent 7.1].

arguments.point: The deviation is 4.3 km against a recommended route of 20.5 km, over the 1 km tolerance.
No message or call told the rider about a reroute before or at the deviation; the driver's only reply came after the rider asked and gave no reason.
The remedy Section 1.3 gives for an unannounced deviation is the excess distance fare, S$3.44, as in Precedent 7.1.

weaknesses.point: The traffic record shows a vehicle fire on the PIE during the trip, so the driver will say the reroute was justified; that limits the remedy to the partial refund.

driver_advocate.stance: The reroute was a response to a real incident on the PIE; only the missing notice is at issue, and the refund must stay limited to the excess distance fare.
driver_advocate.requested_outcome: no refund beyond the excess distance fare; tolls and the rest of the fare stand
driver_advocate.brief: Section 1.1 lets a driver leave the recommended path for real-time traffic. Historical traffic data, which Section 1.4 names as the test, shows a vehicle fire on the PIE eastbound from 13:05 to 13:50 with two lanes blocked [E-TRF-01] and heavy congestion at the PIE airport exit from 13:15 to 13:40 [E-TRF-02]; the trip ran 13:15 to 13:52 [E-TRP-01]. The ECP was flowing freely [E-TRF-03]. So this is the 'rerouted for traffic' row of Section 1.3, and the rider arrived in 37 minutes against an estimate of 35 [E-TRP-01]. When the rider asked, the driver answered within a minute [E-CHT-05] [E-CHT-06]. The only remedy that row gives is a partial refund of the excess distance fare, S$3.44, not the whole S$6.50 difference, and the tolls of S$2.22 pass through at cost [E-PAY-01] [Precedent 7.1].

arguments.point: A vehicle fire and heavy congestion on the PIE overlapped the trip, so the reroute had a traffic justification.
The ECP was flowing smoothly, a reasonable alternative to the blocked PIE.
A justified but unannounced reroute earns the excess distance fare only: S$3.44 of the S$6.50 difference; the S$2.22 of tolls passes through at cost.

rebuttals.reply: The deviation is not disputed, but Section 1.3 gives no refund for distance alone when the reroute is justified by traffic.
The driver reassured the rider within a minute of the question; the reply did not name the reroute, but the rider was never refused an answer.
Agreed that Precedent 7.1 applies; it also shows the refund stops at the excess distance fare.

concessions.point: No chat message or call before or at the deviation told the rider of the reroute and the reason.
The deviation of 4.3 km is over the 1 km tolerance.

arguments.point: A vehicle fire and heavy congestion on the PIE overlapped the trip, so the reroute had a traffic justification.
The ECP was flowing smoothly, a reasonable alternative to the blocked PIE.
A justified but unannounced reroute earns the excess distance fare only: S$3.44 of the S$6.50 difference; the S$2.22 of tolls passes through at cost.

rebuttals.reply: The deviation is not disputed, but Section 1.3 gives no refund for distance alone when the reroute is justified by traffic.
The driver reassured the rider within a minute of the question; the reply did not name the reroute, but the rider was never refused an answer.
Agreed that Precedent 7.1 applies; it also shows the refund stops at the excess distance fare.

concessions.point: No chat message or call before or at the deviation told the rider of the reroute and the reason.
The deviation of 4.3 km is over the 1 km tolerance.

Section 1.2 required notice before or at the point of deviation; the chat holds none, and the driver's reply to the rider's question names neither a reroute nor a reason [E-CHT-05] [E-CHT-06]. Precedent 7.1 ruled the same way. Because the deviation is more than 2 km, a Ryde staff member confirms the refund before it takes effect; you can also ask for a human review.
